tierWindow.goal: Understand what exams are, why they take the forms they do, and why that understanding, together with the anxiety exams provoke, points to the need for a revision strategy.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Understand and recognise (identify, describe, explain why), the entry level of the three tiers: no building or applying a strategy yet.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Single-step recognition and explanation tasks: naming an exam type, explaining a purpose, recognising a feeling.
tierWindow.autonomy: High scaffolding; worked examples model the thinking directly; the learner recognises and explains rather than plans or chooses.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: No assumed prior experience of this pathway (assumesFromPrevious: null at introductory). The learner may already sit exams but has not yet examined why exams exist, what forms they take, or why a strategy is worth having. This tier gives them that understanding; the intermediate tier then has them build a strategy from it.

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has four short lessons. First, why exams exist. Second, the different forms an exam can take. Third, what exam anxiety is actually telling you. Fourth, bringing all three together into one way of approaching any exam you are set. Work through them in order; the last lesson depends on the first three.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the four lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course is about understanding exams before you revise for one. By the end you will be able to explain why universities use exams and what they test that other assessment forms do not, distinguish between the different forms an exam can take, and recognise exam anxiety for what it is rather than something to just push away.

None of this is about technique yet; that comes later in this pathway. It is about seeing an exam clearly enough that preparing for it makes sense.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain why exams exist and what they test, distinguish between exam forms, recognise exam anxiety and why it points to a strategy.

practiceConnection.academic: Understanding what a piece of assessment is actually for, rather than just completing it, is a habit that serves you well beyond exams. The same question, what is this checking and why, is worth asking of any coursework, presentation or report you are set.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate revising and exams course turns this understanding into an actual revision strategy, built around your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge. Going wider: the same habit of asking what a piece of work is actually for underpins Academic Writing, Researching and Reflective Practice.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. An exam is no longer an arbitrary hurdle: you can explain what it tests that other assessment forms do not, tell its different forms apart, and recognise your own anxiety about one as information rather than a flaw. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, the habit of asking what a piece of work is actually testing, and reading your own uncertainty about it as a prompt rather than a problem, is one you can carry into any assessment you face, in your studies and beyond.
